ser-vs-estar.why: Location of people and things takes estar.
Professions take ser.

ser-vs-estar.en: The party is at my house.
ser-vs-estar.why: Where an event takes place uses ser.
A temporary condition takes estar.
Dates and days take ser.
States and moods take estar.
With ser, aburrido means boring. With estar it means bored.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Aburrido: boring with ser, bored with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: Listo means ready with estar and clever with ser.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Listo: clever with ser, ready with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: Even permanent locations take estar.
Muerto takes estar, even though death is permanent.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Muerto takes estar, even though death is permanent

ser-vs-estar.why: Rico means wealthy with ser and delicious with estar.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Rico: wealthy with ser, delicious with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: Actions in progress use estar with the gerund.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Actions in progress, with the gerund

ser-vs-estar.why: Origin takes ser.
A trait that says what someone is like takes ser.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Traits that describe what something is like

ser-vs-estar.why: Time takes ser.
Possession takes ser.

ser-vs-estar.en: The concert is at the stadium.
ser-vs-estar.why: Where an event takes place uses ser.
A place's location takes estar. Only events take ser.
Location of things takes estar.
Being sick is a condition, so estar.

ser-vs-estar.q: Hoy _____ muy nerviosa. (ser or estar, yo)
ser-vs-estar.why: A mood right now takes estar.
An action in progress uses estar with the gerund.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Actions in progress, with the gerund

ser-vs-estar.q: No hay nada que hacer. _____ aburrido.
ser-vs-estar.en: There's nothing to do. I'm bored.
ser-vs-estar.why: With estar, aburrido means bored. Soy aburrido would mean I'm boring.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Aburrido: boring with ser, bored with estar

ser-vs-estar.q: Tu hija _____ muy lista. Siempre saca buenas notas.
ser-vs-estar.en: Your daughter is very clever. She always gets good grades.
ser-vs-estar.why: With ser, listo means clever.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Listo: clever with ser, ready with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: With estar, rico means delicious.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Rico: wealthy with ser, delicious with estar

ser-vs-estar.en: Don't drink that milk. It's gone off.
ser-vs-estar.why: With estar, malo means sick or gone off.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Malo: bad with ser, sick or gone off with estar

ser-vs-estar.q: Ese perro _____ malo. Muerde a todos.
ser-vs-estar.en: That dog is mean. It bites everyone.
ser-vs-estar.why: With ser, malo describes what the dog is like.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Malo: bad with ser, sick or gone off with estar

ser-vs-estar.why: In everyday speech, casado usually takes estar.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Casado usually takes estar in everyday speech

ser-vs-estar.q: Mi mamá _____ contenta con la noticia.
ser-vs-estar.en: My mom is happy about the news.
ser-vs-estar.why: Contento always takes estar.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Contento always takes estar, but feliz can take either

ser-vs-estar.why: Muerto takes estar.
ser-vs-estar.rule: Muerto takes estar, even though death is permanent

ser-vs-estar.why: Origin takes ser.

por-vs-para.why: Movement through or along takes por.

por-vs-para.en: I paid ten dollars for the shirt.
I was late because of the traffic.
I study in order to learn.
I lived there for five years.
I'll call you on the phone.
I work for a big company.
por-vs-para.rule: The choice can change what you're saying

por-vs-para.why: Por fin is a set phrase.
por-vs-para.rule: These are worth memorizing as units

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: Yesterday I ate chicken and rice.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: A completed action takes the preterite.

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: As a child I used to play in the street.
It was ten o'clock when I arrived.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Time in the past takes the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Time and age in the past

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I was sleeping when the phone rang.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: The interruption takes the preterite, and the background takes the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: The imperfect is the background, and the preterite is what happened

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: It was raining when we left.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Leaving is the event, set against the background of the rain.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: The imperfect is the background, and the preterite is what happened

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I lived in Cuba for twenty years.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: A defined period takes the preterite, however long.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: A defined period of time, however long

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: _____ a mi esposa en un baile.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I met my wife at a dance.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Conocer in the preterite means met.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Conocer: met in the preterite, knew in the imperfect

preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Saber in the imperfect means knew. In the preterite it means found out.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Saber: found out in the preterite, knew in the imperfect

preterite-vs-imperfect.en: I was cooking while she was reading.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Two actions in progress both take the imperfect.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Actions in progress in the past

preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Poder in the preterite means managed to.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: Poder: managed to in the preterite, was able to in the imperfect

preterite-vs-imperfect.q: Hacía sol y la playa _____ llena.
preterite-vs-imperfect.en: It was sunny and the beach was full.
preterite-vs-imperfect.why: Description and background take the imperfect.
No querer in the preterite means refused.
preterite-vs-imperfect.rule: No querer in the preterite means refused

subjunctive.why: A wish plus a new subject takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: A trigger in the main clause, then que, then a new subject

subjunctive.why: Creo que states a belief, so it takes the indicative.
No creer expresses doubt, so it takes the subjunctive.
Cuando takes the subjunctive for something that hasn't happened yet.
subjunctive.rule: Time words, when the event hasn't happened yet

subjunctive.q: Cuando _____ a casa, siempre te llamo.
subjunctive.en: When I get home, I always call you.
subjunctive.why: For habits, cuando takes the indicative.
subjunctive.rule: Time words, when the event hasn't happened yet

subjunctive.en: I hope you have a good trip.
I'm looking for an apartment that has a balcony.
subjunctive.why: You haven't found it yet, so it may not exist.
subjunctive.rule: Looking for something that may not exist

subjunctive.en: I have an apartment that has a balcony.
subjunctive.why: A known, real thing takes the indicative.
subjunctive.rule: Looking for something that may not exist

subjunctive.en: If I had money, I would travel.
subjunctive.why: Unreal conditions use si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional.
subjunctive.rule: Unreal conditions: si + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional

subjunctive.why: Antes de que always takes the subjunctive.
subjunctive.rule: Purpose and conditions: para que, a menos que, sin que, antes de que

subjunctive.en: It's true that he's coming tomorrow.
subjunctive.why: Stating a fact takes the indicative.
With no change of subject, use the infinitive.
subjunctive.rule: A trigger in the main clause, then que, then a new subject

gender-and-plurals.why: Día is a masculine exception ending in -a.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Masculine nouns ending in -a, many from Greek and ending in -ma

gender-and-plurals.why: Mano is a feminine exception ending in -o.
Many nouns ending in -ma are masculine.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Masculine nouns ending in -a, many from Greek and ending in -ma

gender-and-plurals.why: Feminine nouns starting with stressed a take el in the singular. The adjective stays feminine.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Feminine nouns starting with a stressed a take el in the singular

gender-and-plurals.why: Mapa is a masculine exception ending in -a.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Masculine nouns ending in -a, many from Greek and ending in -ma

gender-and-plurals.why: Foto is short for fotografía, so it's feminine.

gender-and-plurals.en: one young person, two young people
gender-and-plurals.why: The accent appears to keep the stress on the same syllable.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Accents shift to keep the stress in place

gender-and-plurals.why: The accent drops because the stress is now regular.
gender-and-plurals.rule: Accents shift to keep the stress in place

reflexive-verbs.rule: Me, te, se, nos, and se for ellos and ustedes
Me, te, se, nos, and se for ellos and ustedes

reflexive-verbs.why: The pronoun attaches to the infinitive, or goes before voy.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Attached to an infinitive or gerund, or before the verb in front of it

reflexive-verbs.why: Body parts take the, because the pronoun already shows whose they are.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Body parts and clothing take the, not my
Ir to go, irse to leave

reflexive-verbs.why: Accidents use se, so the thing happens to you.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Accidents: the thing happens to you

reflexive-verbs.why: Negative commands put the pronoun before the verb.
Parecerse a means to look like.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Parecer to seem, parecerse a to look like

reflexive-verbs.why: Impersonal se means people in general.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Impersonal: people in general, or no specific person

reflexive-verbs.en: We hugged each other at the airport.
reflexive-verbs.why: Plural reflexives can mean each other.

reflexive-verbs.en: I fell asleep at the movies.
reflexive-verbs.rule: Dormir to sleep, dormirse to fall asleep

reflexive-verbs.why: Casarse is reflexive, and ella takes se.

object-pronouns.en: I bought the book. I bought it.
object-pronouns.why: Libro is a masculine direct object.
object-pronouns.rule: Direct objects: me, te, lo, la, nos, los, las

object-pronouns.en: I see María. I see her.
object-pronouns.why: María is a feminine direct object.
object-pronouns.rule: Direct objects: me, te, lo, la, nos, los, las

object-pronouns.why: Mi hijo receives the money, so he's the indirect object.
object-pronouns.rule: Indirect objects: me, te, le, nos, les

object-pronouns.why: Le changes to se before lo.
object-pronouns.rule: Le and les change to se before lo, la, los, las

object-pronouns.why: Lo is the thing given, and it comes after the indirect pronoun.
The pronoun attaches to the infinitive, or goes before voy.
object-pronouns.rule: Attached to an infinitive or gerund, or before the verb in front of it
Attached to affirmative commands, before negative ones

object-pronouns.why: A specific person as a direct object takes the personal a.

object-pronouns.why: The things liked are the subject, so the verb is plural.
object-pronouns.rule: Gustar works backward: the thing liked is the subject

object-pronouns.why: Gustar takes an indirect pronoun, even when the person is named.
object-pronouns.rule: Gustar works backward: the thing liked is the subject

object-pronouns.q: _____ escribí una carta a mis padres.
object-pronouns.en: I wrote my parents a letter.
object-pronouns.why: Mis padres are the indirect object, and they're plural.
object-pronouns.rule: Indirect objects: me, te, le, nos, les

object-pronouns.rule: Usted and ustedes use the third-person pronouns

commands.why: Affirmative tú commands use the él form of the present.
commands.rule: Affirmative: use the él form of the present

commands.why: Negative tú commands use the present subjunctive.
Decir has the short form di.
commands.rule: Eight verbs have short affirmative forms: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven

commands.why: Hacer has the short form haz.
commands.rule: Eight verbs have short affirmative forms: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven

commands.why: Ir has the short form ve.

commands.why: Venir has the short form ven.
commands.rule: Eight verbs have short affirmative forms: di, haz, ve, pon, sal, sé, ten, ven

commands.why: Negative commands use the subjunctive, even for the eight short verbs.
Usted commands use the present subjunctive.

commands.rule: Ustedes is the plural for everyone in Latin America
Ir uses vamos, and vámonos with a pronoun

commands.why: Pronouns attach to affirmative commands, often adding an accent.
commands.rule: Pronouns attach to affirmative commands, often adding a written accent

Poner has the short form pon.

perfect-tenses.rule: Conjugate haber, and the participle never changes

perfect-tenses.why: The participle never changes after haber.
perfect-tenses.rule: Conjugate haber, and the participle never changes

perfect-tenses.why: Él takes ha, and pronouns go before haber.
perfect-tenses.rule: Nothing goes between haber and the participle

perfect-tenses.why: Latin America usually prefers the preterite for recent events.
perfect-tenses.rule: Latin America usually prefers the preterite for recent events

perfect-tenses.why: Life experience uses the present perfect, with the participle ido.
perfect-tenses.rule: The present perfect is natural for life experience

perfect-tenses.en: If I had studied, I would have passed.

perfect-tenses.rule: Si + pluperfect subjunctive, then the conditional perfect

perfect-tenses.why: With estar, the participle acts as an adjective and agrees.
perfect-tenses.rule: With estar the participle acts as an adjective and agrees

perfect-tenses.why: After haber, the participle doesn't change.
Acabar de + infinitive means have just.
perfect-tenses.rule: Acabar de + infinitive means have just

comparisons.q: Mi hermano es más alto _____ yo.
comparisons.en: My brother is taller than me.
I have more than twenty cousins.
comparisons.rule: Use de, not que, before a number

comparisons.q: Ana es tan alta _____ su madre.
comparisons.en: Ana is as tall as her mother.
I don't have as many shirts as he does.
comparisons.rule: Tanto + noun + como, agreeing with the noun

comparisons.en: This coffee is better than that one.
comparisons.rule: Bueno becomes mejor, and malo becomes peor

comparisons.en: My older sister lives in Ponce.

comparisons.q: Es la playa más bonita _____ la isla.
comparisons.en: It's the prettiest beach on the island.
comparisons.rule: El, la, los or las + más + adjective + de

comparisons.q: Es el _____ restaurante de la ciudad.
comparisons.en: It's the best restaurant in the city.
comparisons.why: With mejor and peor, no más is needed.
comparisons.rule: With mejor and peor, no más is needed

comparisons.en: I don't work as much as before.
comparisons.rule: Verb + tanto como, with no agreement

comparisons.en: You speak as fast as I do.
comparisons.why: Tan goes with adjectives and adverbs.
The adverb bien also becomes mejor.
comparisons.rule: Bien becomes mejor, and mal becomes peor, as adverbs

comparisons.why: Rico adds -ísimo, the spelling changes to qu, and it agrees with comida.

talking-about-the-future.en: I'm going to eat.
talking-about-the-future.why: The pattern is ir a + infinitive.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Conjugate ir, add a, then the infinitive

talking-about-the-future.en: There's going to be a party.
talking-about-the-future.why: Hay becomes va a haber, always singular.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Hay becomes va a haber

talking-about-the-future.en: I'll call you when I arrive.
talking-about-the-future.why: A future event after cuando takes the subjunctive.
talking-about-the-future.rule: After cuando and similar words, a future event takes the subjunctive, not the future

talking-about-the-future.en: I wonder what time it is.
talking-about-the-future.why: The simple future can express a guess about now.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Guessing about the present

talking-about-the-future.en: I'm leaving for Bogotá tomorrow.
talking-about-the-future.why: The present works for plans with a time word.

talking-about-the-future.en: I'll always love you.
talking-about-the-future.why: Promises use the simple future.

talking-about-the-future.en: My kids are going to arrive soon.
talking-about-the-future.why: Ir agrees with the subject.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Conjugate ir, add a, then the infinitive

talking-about-the-future.q: _____ a llamarte, pero se me olvidó.
talking-about-the-future.en: I was going to call you, but I forgot.

talking-about-the-future.rule: Iba a + infinitive: was going to

talking-about-the-future.en: He said he would come.
talking-about-the-future.why: The conditional reports what someone said would happen.
talking-about-the-future.rule: The conditional reports what someone said would happen

talking-about-the-future.en: I'm going to call you.
talking-about-the-future.why: Pronouns can go before the conjugated ir.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Pronouns go before ir or attach to the infinitive

talking-about-the-future.en: It will rain across the whole island tomorrow.
talking-about-the-future.why: Forecasts use the simple future.
talking-about-the-future.rule: News, forecasts and formal plans

talking-about-the-future.en: It must be about two.
talking-about-the-future.why: The future of ser can express a guess about the time.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Guessing about the present

talking-about-the-future.en: We're going to travel in May.
talking-about-the-future.why: Ir agrees with nosotros: vamos a.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Conjugate ir, add a, then the infinitive

talking-about-the-future.q: ¿_____ a venir a la fiesta? (ir, tú)
talking-about-the-future.en: Are you going to come to the party?
talking-about-the-future.why: Ir for tú is vas.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Conjugate ir, add a, then the infinitive

talking-about-the-future.en: They're going to buy a car.
talking-about-the-future.why: It's always ir a plus the infinitive.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Conjugate ir, add a, then the infinitive

talking-about-the-future.en: Tomorrow I'm going to go to the market.
talking-about-the-future.why: After ir a comes the infinitive, even when it's ir again.
talking-about-the-future.rule: It's the normal choice in conversation

talking-about-the-future.en: Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.
talking-about-the-future.why: Ir a plus the infinitive is the everyday way to say what's coming.
talking-about-the-future.rule: It's the normal choice in conversation

talking-about-the-future.en: I'm going to call you later.
talking-about-the-future.why: After the infinitive, the pronoun attaches to it.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Pronouns go before ir or attach to the infinitive

talking-about-the-future.en: There are going to be a lot of people.
talking-about-the-future.why: Va a haber stays singular, like hay.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Hay becomes va a haber

talking-about-the-future.en: The flight leaves at eight.
talking-about-the-future.why: Schedules use the present.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Use the present for plans and schedules, with a time word

talking-about-the-future.en: Shall I help you?
talking-about-the-future.why: Offers use the present.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Offers and suggestions also use the present

talking-about-the-future.en: I'll call you later.
talking-about-the-future.why: A quick promise like this uses the present.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Offers and suggestions also use the present

talking-about-the-future.en: I'll pay you on Friday.
talking-about-the-future.why: A promise often takes the simple future.
talking-about-the-future.rule: Promises and strong intentions

talking-about-the-future.en: Tomorrow it will be sunny on the coast.
talking-about-the-future.why: Forecasts use the simple future.
talking-about-the-future.rule: News, forecasts and formal plans

talking-about-the-future.en: I wonder where my phone is.
talking-about-the-future.why: The simple future can guess about now.

relative-pronouns.q: El hombre _____ vive aquí es mi tío.

relative-pronouns.rule: Use que for people and things

relative-pronouns.q: El libro _____ leí es muy bueno.

relative-pronouns.rule: It can't be left out, even when English drops that

relative-pronouns.en: The friends I invited didn't come.

numbers-and-dates.rule: Uno shortens before a masculine noun and changes before a feminine one

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Adjectives ending in a consonant add -es.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Adjectives ending in -e or a consonant only change for the plural

nouns-and-adjectives.why: A final z becomes c in the plural.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: A final z becomes c

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Adjectives ending in -or add -a for the feminine.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Nationalities and words ending in -or add -a

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Bueno drops the -o before a masculine noun.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Bueno and malo drop the -o before a masculine noun, and grande becomes gran

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Before a noun, grande becomes gran and means great.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Bueno and malo drop the -o before a masculine noun, and grande becomes gran

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Mi adds -s for a plural noun.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Mi, tu and su add -s for a plural noun

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Esto is for something you can't name yet.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Esto and eso for ideas, or things you can't name

nouns-and-adjectives.why: A profession after ser doesn't take un or una.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Spanish uses 'the' where English doesn't

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Día is masculine, despite the -a.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Some common ones break the pattern

nouns-and-adjectives.en: I'm looking for a map of the city.
nouns-and-adjectives.why: Mapa is masculine, despite the -a.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Some common ones break the pattern

nouns-and-adjectives.en: My friend Ana lives in Quito.
nouns-and-adjectives.why: Ana is a woman, so amigo becomes amiga.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Nouns for people often have both forms

nouns-and-adjectives.q: La _____ de matemáticas es muy buena.
nouns-and-adjectives.en: The math teacher (a woman) is very good.
nouns-and-adjectives.why: Profesor adds -a for a woman.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Nouns for people often have both forms

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Mesas is feminine plural, so las.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: 'The': el, la, los, las

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Manzanas is feminine plural, so unas.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: 'A' and 'some': un, una, unos, unas

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Spanish uses el for things in general, where English uses no article.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Spanish uses 'the' where English doesn't

nouns-and-adjectives.why: With days, el already means on.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Spanish uses 'the' where English doesn't

nouns-and-adjectives.why: After a consonant, add -es.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Add -s after a vowel and -es after a consonant

nouns-and-adjectives.en: Juan and María are my siblings.
nouns-and-adjectives.why: A mixed group of men and women takes the masculine.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: A mixed group takes the masculine

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Nationalities ending in a consonant add -a for the feminine.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Nationalities and words ending in -or add -a

nouns-and-adjectives.en: We live in a white house.
nouns-and-adjectives.why: Adjectives usually go after the noun.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Usually after the noun

nouns-and-adjectives.en: There are a lot of people in the park.
nouns-and-adjectives.why: Words for how many go before the noun.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Numbers and words for how many go before

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Malo drops the -o before a masculine noun.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Bueno and malo drop the -o before a masculine noun, and grande becomes gran

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Nuestro agrees with the noun, and familia is feminine.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Nuestro agrees like any adjective ending in -o

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Tu adds -s for a plural noun.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Mi, tu and su add -s for a plural noun

nouns-and-adjectives.why: When su could mean his or her, say de ella after the noun.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Su can mean 'his', 'her', 'its', 'their' or 'your'

nouns-and-adjectives.en: Do you see that mountain, way over there?
nouns-and-adjectives.why: Aquella is for something far from both of you.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Este for 'this' and 'these', ese for 'that' and 'those', aquel for 'that over there'

nouns-and-adjectives.en: Which one do you prefer, this one or that one?
nouns-and-adjectives.why: On its own, esa means that one. Eso is for ideas.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: On their own, they mean 'this one' or 'that one'

nouns-and-adjectives.why: Eso is for an idea, not a thing you can name.
nouns-and-adjectives.rule: Esto and eso for ideas, or things you can't name

idioms.why: Hunger is tener hambre, and very is mucha.
idioms.rule: Hunger, thirst, sleepiness, cold, heat, fear and hurry

idioms.why: To be right is tener razón.
To feel like is tener ganas de.
idioms.rule: Tener ganas de: to feel like

idioms.why: To be needed is hacer falta.
To be worth it is valer la pena.
idioms.rule: Valer la pena: to be worth it

idioms.en: I get along well with my mother-in-law.
idioms.why: To get along is llevarse bien.
idioms.rule: Llevarse bien or mal: to get along, or not

idioms.why: To put your foot in it is meter la pata.
idioms.rule: Meter la pata: to put your foot in it

idioms.why: To pull someone's leg is tomar el pelo.
idioms.rule: Tomar el pelo: to pull someone's leg

idioms.why: To agree is estar de acuerdo.
Most of Latin America says extrañar for to miss.
idioms.rule: Extrañar: to miss someone or something

idioms.why: The keys are the subject, so the verb is plural.
idioms.rule: Se, then me, te or le, then the verb, for accidents

idioms.why: The saying is más vale tarde que nunca.
idioms.rule: Refranes come up all the time, often only the first half

idioms.q: Ese carro cuesta un ojo de la _____.
idioms.en: That car costs an arm and a leg.
idioms.why: The expression is costar un ojo de la cara.
idioms.rule: Costar un ojo de la cara: to cost an arm and a leg

idioms.why: Las alturas is the subject, so dan.
idioms.rule: Me da igual, me da miedo, me da pena

por-vs-para-basics.en: This coffee is for you.
por-vs-para-basics.why: Who something is for takes para.

por-vs-para-basics.en: I study to learn.
Tomorrow I leave for Lima.
por-vs-para-basics.why: Where someone is headed takes para.

por-vs-para-basics.en: The homework is for Friday.
For me, Spanish is easy.
Thanks for everything.
I'm always late because of the traffic.
We walk through the park.
por-vs-para-basics.why: Through or along a place takes por.

por-vs-para-basics.en: I'm paying twenty dollars for the shoes.
I'll call you on the phone.
por-vs-para-basics.why: How you get in touch takes por.

por-vs-para-basics.en: I work in the morning.
por-vs-para-basics.why: Parts of the day take por.

por-vs-para-basics.en: "Why are you studying Spanish?" "Because I like it."
por-vs-para-basics.why: ¿Por qué? asks why, and porque answers.
por-vs-para-basics.rule: ¿Por qué? asks why, and porque answers

por-vs-para-basics.en: Please, can you help me?
por-vs-para-basics.why: Por favor is a set phrase.

por-vs-para-basics.en: I work to earn money.
Is this present for me?
por-vs-para-basics.why: Who something is for takes para.

por-vs-para-basics.q: El bus sale _____ Quito a las diez.
por-vs-para-basics.en: The bus leaves for Quito at ten.
I need the report by tomorrow.

por-vs-para-basics.q: _____ mi papá, el béisbol es el mejor deporte.
por-vs-para-basics.en: For my dad, baseball is the best sport.
I'm not going out because of the rain.
por-vs-para-basics.why: The rain is the reason, so por.

por-vs-para-basics.en: Thanks so much for the invitation.
We stroll around downtown.
por-vs-para-basics.why: Through or around a place is por.

por-vs-para-basics.en: The cat comes in through the window.

por-vs-para-basics.q: Te cambio mi sándwich _____ tu manzana.
por-vs-para-basics.en: I'll trade you my sandwich for your apple.
How much are you paying for the car?
I'll send you the photo by email.
por-vs-para-basics.why: How you get in touch takes por.

por-vs-para-basics.en: I study at night.
por-vs-para-basics.why: A part of the day with no clock time takes por.

por-vs-para-basics.en: It's raining a lot. That's why I'm not going out.
It's Friday at last!

por-vs-para-basics.q: —¿Por qué no comes? —_____ no tengo hambre.
por-vs-para-basics.en: "Why aren't you eating?" "Because I'm not hungry."
por-vs-para-basics.why: ¿Por qué? asks why, and porque answers.
por-vs-para-basics.rule: ¿Por qué? asks why, and porque answers

por-vs-para-basics.en: I'm buying flowers for my mom.
por-vs-para-basics.why: The flowers go to her, so para.
por-vs-para-basics.rule: A goal or destination takes para, and a reason or route takes por

por-vs-para-basics.en: I'm here because of my mom.
por-vs-para-basics.why: She's the reason you're here, so por.
por-vs-para-basics.rule: A goal or destination takes para, and a reason or route takes por
